**This run cannot confirm the premise: both starting leads timed out, so the collected evidence cannot verify that OpenAI's annualized revenue is near $50 billion, cannot resolve the metric or accounting basis, and cannot connect any such report to an AI-stock selloff.**

### What the tools returned

- **agt_2** (`research.open_page` on the Axios URL) failed with `TimeoutError: research.open_page timed out after 40s`.
- **agt_3** (`research.open_page` on the FT URL) failed with `TimeoutError: research.open_page timed out after 40s`.
- **agt_1** (`research.live_event_evidence`) completed, but returned only provider headlines and snippets, not article bodies. It also reported `live_event_impact_map timed out after 4s` and `Skipped remaining symbol news searches because the live-event budget was exhausted.`

No OpenAI revenue figure was read at source. The ~$70 billion September figure and the ~$50 billion October figure remain user-supplied claims in this run.

### Metric and accounting distinctions that matter

The gap between an old and a new revenue number can come from four different causes. Each cause has a different meaning.

- **Annualized run-rate (ARR)** is a snapshot: a recent month or quarter multiplied by twelve. It is not audited revenue and not a forecast. A change of base month alone can move the number.
- **Gross versus net basis.** Gross counts the full value of usage that flows through the product. Net counts only the company's own share after payments to cloud hosts, model partners, or publishers. A move from gross to net lowers the headline without lowering cash collected.
- **Partner or reseller accounting.** Revenue may be booked when a cloud marketplace or reseller bills the end customer, or when the end customer pays. Whether the partner markup is included also changes the total.
- **Definition change.** A switch from annualized to trailing, or from a full-year estimate to a current run-rate, produces two numbers that are not comparable.

Only a change in the same metric, on the same basis, over the same window shows a real sales decline. The current evidence does not allow that test.

### Market check: the selloff claim is not measured

No price series, daily movers table, or index move was collected in this run. The only current item is a Seeking Alpha headline dated **2026-10-08**, "Nvidia: The Top AI Stock Is On Sale (NASDAQ:NVDA)", whose snippet says the forward multiple is near decade lows. A second item (Seeking Alpha, **2026-10-07**) covers **ORCL** earnings acceleration, and a third (Investor's Business Daily, **2026-10-07**) covers **MSFT** sales and profit growth. These are headline fragments, not observed market data. The run has not collected enough current evidence to state that an AI-stock selloff is under way today, let alone to attribute it to the OpenAI report.

### Why the distinction could matter, if confirmed

Gross-to-net restatement is a reporting change, not a demand change. It would lower the headline figure while customer spend stays flat. A real decline would appear as lower bookings, lower usage, or lower cash receipts on a consistent basis. An investor who treats a restated number as lost sales would misprice the news. An investor who dismisses it without checking the basis could miss a genuine slowdown. The current evidence does not separate these cases.

### What to check next

- Read the FT article (https://www.ft.com/content/b66a9858-f8fb-46cb-b506-44bfe26fca2a) and the Axios article (https://www.axios.com/2026/10/08/openai-50-billion-arr-anthropic-revenue-accounting) directly. Record the exact metric label, the basis (gross or net), and the base month for each figure.
- Check whether the September ~$70 billion figure was an ARR, a full-year 2026 estimate, or a forward projection. Different definitions can explain the gap without any demand change.
- Pull same-day index and single-stock price data for **NVDA**, **MSFT**, **ORCL**, and **AMD** before linking the report to a selloff.
- Ask OpenAI or its partners for a statement on accounting basis and partner-revenue treatment.

**Takeaway: treat the $50 billion versus $70 billion comparison as unresolved. The source reads and the price data are missing from this run.**
